The spring of 2030 came early to Florence, with the wisteria already in bloom at the end of March along the walls of via Maggio and the swallows coming back to nest under the eaves of Santo Spirito. In the trattoria, Karl’s kitchen had been going for three months. At first the regular customers came in warily, looked towards the counter, searched for Graziella with their eyes, and when they didn’t find her tasted the ribollita with a suspicious air, the way you taste a new neighbour’s wine. Then, one after another, they stopped looking for her. Karl got up every morning at five, lit Ion’s lantern above the stove and began. He had changed very little: he had added a Maltese dish on Fridays, his mother’s pastizzi, and had had Davide paint a blue eye on the kitchen door, like the ones on the boats of Marsaxlokk, to protect those who worked there. Otherwise, everything was as before. Even the hug. Karl gave it to those who ordered the ribollita abbracciosa, clumsy and serious, and after a while the customers began to say it wasn’t bad. Guido said it was “a hug with an accent”, and that he liked it anyway.

Graziella, on the other hand, had discovered retirement the way you discover a foreign country: with curiosity, a little fear, and the feeling of not quite understanding the language. The first days she still woke at five, out of habit, and lay in bed looking at the ceiling, listening to the noises of Karl’s kitchen downstairs. Then, little by little, she learned. She learned to sleep until seven. She learned to have breakfast sitting down, with the newspaper, instead of standing between one stove and another. She learned to walk with no destination, something she had never done in seventy-five years. And she learned to watch sunsets. Every evening at seven she went up to the terrace in via della Chiesa with Doina’s honey-coloured shawl on her shoulders, sat on the wicker chair next to Totò’s pot and watched the sun go down behind the hills of Bellosguardo. Viola often kept her company. They didn’t talk much. One evening Viola asked her why she watched the sun every evening, since it was always the same. Graziella thought about it. “It’s never the same,” she said. “I’m the one who didn’t notice for fifty years.”

On Sunday mornings, though, the kitchen became hers again. That was the rule she had kept: she made the Sunday ribollita, and nobody else. But she no longer made it alone. Viola, who would turn seven in May, arrived at eight in the little apron Doina had sewn for her, with Assunta’s thimble on her thumb for luck, and climbed onto the stool next to the table. Graziella taught her everything, one step at a time, as she had promised. How to strip the black cabbage, removing the tough rib. How to cut the carrots and celery for the soffritto, tiny tiny, “like confetti”. Why the beans are salted only at the end. Why the bread has to be two days old, and unsalted. And at the end, when everything was almost ready, Viola went on tiptoe to the window above the sink, picked a leaf from Aldo’s plant, smelled it, and put it in the pot. It was her job. Nobody, not even Karl, touched it. One Sunday in April, Graziella tasted Viola’s ribollita, which she had made almost entirely on her own, and was silent. Then she said: “Eight and a half.” It was the highest mark she had ever given anyone who wasn’t Aldo.

Pietro and Bianca, meanwhile, had been together for four months, and the neighbourhood had known for four months and a day. Not much had changed, on the surface. They kept arguing about words, transcribing interviews in the green notebook, walking up to Arcetri on Sunday afternoons to look down on Florence. Bianca was preparing her final-exam project, which she would present in June: she had chosen as her subject “The words that are disappearing: Florentine in the sound archive of the National Library”, and Guido had become her official informant, with a laminated badge he showed to everyone. Pietro, who would take his final exams the following year, had started writing seriously. Not just the black notebook: a book. It told the story of via Maggio, from 1950 to today, through the people who had lived there: Renzo and Lucia opening the trattoria, Aldo with the red bicycle, Graziella with the ladle, Matei and Giulia with their brushes, Viola with the thimble. He didn’t yet know how it would end. Bellini, who read a chapter a week with his red pencil, told him not to hurry. “Books end when they decide to,” he said. “Like restorations.”

In mid-May the phone call came from Naples. It was Dr Esposito of the Diocesan Museum: the maintenance restoration of the Madonna of the seamstresses was almost finished, and Assunta’s fragment would be put back in the frame the following Saturday, the eighteenth of May, at eleven in the morning. The museum had decided to make a small ceremony of it, with the bishop, the press and the seamstresses of the Vergini quarter, of whom only a few were left but who still brought flowers to the Madonna, now in the museum, on the first Saturday of every month. Giulia phoned Sorrento at once. Rosaria answered, in a worried voice. She said Grandma had been ill that winter: a nasty bronchitis in February, and then a tiredness that wouldn’t go away. She hardly left the house any more. The doctor had advised her not to travel. Giulia was silent. Then she asked to speak to Assunta. There was a long pause, voices in the background, the scrape of a chair. Then her grandmother’s voice, thin but very clear: “I said I’d be there in May,” said Assunta. “And I keep my promises. Let the doctor say what he likes.”

They left Florence on Friday on the seven o’clock train: Giulia, Matei, Viola, Pietro, and Graziella, who had promised Assunta under the pergola that they would see each other in May, and who kept her promises too, as her father had taught her. Dr Neri had given permission, but had written another note: “No stairs. No overly strong emotions.” Graziella had read the second sentence and laughed. On Saturday morning in Naples, the museum at Donnaregina was full. There were the bishop, Dr Esposito, the young restorer in white gloves, the journalists, about twenty elderly seamstresses with bunches of flowers, and the relatives from Sorrento, Rosaria and Gennaro with his family. Assunta arrived last, at five to eleven, in a wheelchair pushed by Gennaro. She wore her black shawl, had her rosary between her fingers and the little lozenge tin clutched in her lap. She was even smaller than the previous autumn, almost transparent. But when they brought her in front of the Madonna of the seamstresses, her black eyes lit up like a little girl’s. “Here I am,” she said to the Madonna. “I told you so.”

The ceremony was short, as Assunta had asked. The bishop said a few words about memory and patience. Dr Esposito told the journalists the story of 1943, the story of the little tin box, and that of the two great-grandmothers under the pergola. Then the restorer went over to Assunta and asked whether she wanted to hand her the fragment with her own hands. Assunta opened the little box. She took the little gold flower with two trembling fingers and looked at it one last time, for a long while, the way you look at a child leaving forever. Then, instead of giving it to the restorer, she turned to Viola, who was standing beside her with the silver thimble on her thumb, and placed it in the little girl’s hand. “You take it,” she told her. “My hands shake. Yours don’t.” Viola looked at the flower, then at her great-grandmother, then at her mother. Giulia nodded, her eyes shining. Viola walked up to the restorer, very slowly, holding the flower in her open palm the way you hold a bird fallen from its nest, and handed it to her. The restorer took it, knelt in front of the frame and, with a tiny brush and a drop of glue, put it back in the hollow of the lower right corner. It took thirty seconds. Eighty-seven years and thirty seconds.

When the restorer stood up, the frame was whole. Twenty little gold flowers, five on each side, all alike. Nobody, looking at the Madonna, could have said which one had spent eighty-seven years in a lozenge tin in Sorrento. Except Assunta, who stared at it without blinking. The seamstresses began to sing, softly, an old Neapolitan song Pietro didn’t know, and laid their flowers in front of the painting, one by one. Graziella, beside the wheelchair, held Assunta’s hand. The two great-grandmothers said nothing for a long time. Then Assunta spoke, very quietly, and Pietro, who was behind them, heard her. “It’s come home,” she said. “Now I can go too.” Graziella squeezed her hand harder. “Don’t talk nonsense,” she told her. “In August you’re coming to Florence. I’ll make you ribollita. No, my granddaughter will make it for you, she’s better than me.” Assunta laughed, a laugh as light as a breath. “Magari,” she said. Then she corrected herself, as in September. “No. No magari. I’ll come. Come what may.” But Pietro saw that Graziella, turning away, wiped her eyes with the back of her hand.

Before leaving for Sorrento, Assunta called Viola over to the wheelchair. She gave her the little lozenge tin, the one in which the flower had stayed for eighty-seven years, now empty, with only the tuft of yellowed cotton wool inside. Viola opened it and looked inside, disappointed. She asked why it was empty. Assunta smiled. She explained that an empty box is the most precious thing in the world, because you can put whatever you want in it. She told her to keep it. And one day to put in it something to look after for someone else, until that someone came to take it back. “You won’t find it straight away,” she said. “It will take years. But when you find it, you’ll know.” Viola closed the box carefully and put it in her dress pocket, next to the thimble. On the train home she didn’t let go of it for a moment. Halfway, between Rome and Florence, Pietro saw her open it secretly, look inside and close it again. He asked her what she had put in it. Viola shook her head, serious. “Nothing yet,” she said. “I’m waiting.” Pietro thought he had just heard the wisest sentence of the whole day, spoken by a seven-year-old girl with chocolate on her chin.

On the seventeenth of May, the day before the ceremony, Viola had turned seven. They celebrated in Sorrento, under the pergola, with a lemon cake made by Rosaria and seven little candles that Viola blew out in a single breath, closing her eyes to make a wish she refused to reveal to anyone. But they made the notch in Florence, when they got back, on Sunday evening, on the door frame of her room, as always. Viola leaned against the frame, barefoot, and Matei drew the line in pencil: one metre nineteen. Next to the notch, Viola wanted to write the date herself, in her still uncertain handwriting, and beneath it, after thinking, she added one word: “Napoli”. Matei asked her why. Viola explained that this year she had grown up in Naples, because she had carried the flower. Matei looked at the door frame: Marco’s notches, from 1978 to 1991; Pietro’s, now almost at the top; the strange one at heart height, “Ha capito”; Graziella’s very low one, “Ricomincia”; and now Viola’s, “Napoli”. He thought that door frame had become a book. A book read from the bottom up, which nobody had finished writing.

It was Viola who, a week later, asked Pietro to take her to the Uffizi. Not to see just any painting: she wanted to see “the angel who laughs”, the one everyone talked about, Davide’s and Mr Alberto’s, the one Grandpa Aldo had shown Nonna Graziella the day before their wedding. Pietro was silent for a moment. Then he remembered an evening in March the year before, when he had come back from the Uffizi after the “Guides for a day” event, and Bellini, in front of the same Madonna, had told him something he had written down at once in the black notebook: “One day you’ll bring a child here. And you’ll say to them ‘look’. That’s all it takes.” Back then he was fifteen, and it had seemed an old man’s sentence, something very far away, to do when he was grown up. Now he was almost seventeen, and a seven-year-old girl was tugging his sleeve asking him to take her to the angel. Pietro understood that the moment had come, even though he didn’t feel at all grown up. He said yes. Then, without telling Viola, he sent Bellini a message: “Saturday at ten. Filippo Lippi room. If you’d like to come.”

On Saturday morning the Uffizi was full of tourists, but the Filippo Lippi room, at ten, was almost empty. Pietro and Viola went in holding hands. Viola wore the yellow-flowered dress from Sorrento and the thimble on her thumb, and walked on tiptoe, the way you walk in church. They stopped in front of the Lippina. The Madonna in profile, with her transparent veil and pearls in her hair, her hands joined. The child leaning towards her. And the angel at the bottom, the rascal, looking out of the painting with that sly smile, as if he knew a secret. Next to the painting, on a wooden lectern, was Davide’s relief reproduction, with its plaque in braille and in Italian. Pietro knelt down beside Viola, at her eye level, as Bellini had done with him the year before in the same place. He prepared no speech. He didn’t explain who Filippo Lippi was, or when the painting was made, or why it was important. He just pointed at the angel with his finger, without touching it, and said a single word. “Guarda.”

Viola looked. She looked for a very long time, for a seven-year-old, almost three minutes, without speaking, without moving, her mouth slightly open. Pietro said nothing. He waited. Then Viola turned to him and said quietly, the way you tell a secret: “He’s laughing because he knows we’re looking at him.” Pietro felt something tighten in his chest. It was exactly what Davide had said a year before, when he discovered the reflection of the window in the angel’s eye: that the angel was looking out of the painting, towards whoever was looking at him. Viola had got there on her own. Then the little girl pointed at Davide’s reproduction on the lectern. She asked whether that one could be touched. And Pietro, who had prepared himself to say the second half of Ernesto’s sentence, “and don’t touch anything”, realised he couldn’t say it. The rules had changed. Ernesto had taught people to look without touching. Davide had taught people to touch for those who couldn’t look. “That one, yes,” said Pietro. “That one’s made for it. Close your eyes.” Viola closed her eyes, put her hands on the relief and began to search, with her fingers, for the angel’s smile.

It was at that moment that Pietro noticed Bellini. He was standing in the doorway of the room, leaning against the frame, his hat in his hand, watching them. Who knew how long he had been there. Pietro stood up and went to meet him. Bellini asked him whether he remembered what he had asked him, a year before, right there. Pietro answered that yes, he remembered: that one day he would bring a child in front of that painting and say to them “look”. Bellini said he had thought it would take him twenty years. Pietro said that if Viola hadn’t asked him herself, maybe he would have waited longer. Then he told him about the changed rules, about the second half of the sentence he hadn’t been able to say, about Davide’s copy that could be touched. Bellini listened in silence. He looked at Viola, who, eyes closed, was stroking the cheeks of the relief angel, smiling. Then he said, his voice trembling: “Then the circle closes. Ernesto would have laughed. And then he would have been moved.” Pietro looked at him. Bellini’s eyes were full of tears and he did nothing to hide them. “Like you are now, professor,” said Pietro softly. Bellini laughed and wiped his eyes with his handkerchief.

They left the Uffizi all three together, at noon, in the May sunshine that made the Arno gleam like a blade. Viola walked in the middle, holding Pietro’s hand on one side and Bellini’s on the other, and every now and then had herself lifted for a jump. On the Ponte Vecchio they stopped to buy ice cream. Bellini told Viola how he, at five, had come out of the Uffizi with his grandfather Ernesto in 1969, and they had stopped on the same bridge, and his grandfather had bought him a lemon ice cream and told him that one day he would understand why he had brought him there. “And did you understand?” asked Viola, her mouth smeared with chocolate. Bellini thought about it. “It took me sixty years,” he said. “I understood today.” Viola asked what he had understood. Bellini bent down to her. “That beautiful things don’t belong to those who own them,” he said. “They belong to those who look at them. And to those who teach others to look.” Viola considered this answer very seriously. Then she announced that in that case she too, when she grew up, would bring a child to see the angel. Bellini and Pietro looked at each other over her head. Neither of them could say anything.

That evening Pietro told Davide everything, at the bar below the workshop. He told him about Viola closing her eyes and searching with her fingers for the angel’s smile, and how she had found it on her own, on the cheeks, exactly where Davide had put it a year before after weeks of prototypes. Davide listened without a word, stirring his coffee. Then he took his museum badge out of his wallet, the one with his photo and name, which the Uffizi had renewed in January. Under the name, where a year before it had said “consultant”, there was now another word. “Tattigrafo”. The accessibility manager had asked the personnel office to change it, after hearing Davide use it for a whole year with everyone, from the guards to the director. It was the first time the word had appeared on an official document. Davide said that in September he would start the summer course at the Opificio delle Pietre Dure, the one for high-school students, and that the professor, reading his application, had asked him what a tattigrafo was. “And what did you tell him?” asked Pietro. Davide smiled. “That it’s a well-formed word,” he said. “And that it should be given to as many people as possible.”

On the second of June 2030 the trattoria turned eighty. Renzo and Lucia had opened it on the second of June 1950, Republic Day, in an old carpenter’s workshop, with four tables, a wood-fired kitchen and a single recipe: Lucia’s ribollita. To celebrate, Karl and Graziella decided to do something that had never been done: take the trattoria out into the square. The City Council gave permission, thanks to Valeria Conti, who had by then been a councillor for three years. In piazza Santo Spirito, under the plane trees, they set up a table sixty metres long, made of all the trattoria’s tables, those lent by the bars in the square, and old doors laid on trestles, as they used to do at neighbourhood festivals in the old days. Three hundred people sat at it. The whole Oltrarno was there. And there, having come from far away, were all those who had passed through via Maggio over those years: Ion and Doina from Sibiu, Ilinca and Radu from Brașov with the children, Chiara Benedetti with her colleagues from the Ernesto cooperative, Turi and Concetta from Syracuse, Dr Camilleri from Malta with Karl’s mother, Andrei with Ioana, Gianni from Bologna, Mr Alberto with his dog.

And Assunta was there. Nobody had really believed it, not even Rosaria. But Assunta had said “I’ll come, come what may”, and on the first of June she had boarded the train to Florence with Rosaria and Gennaro, in her wheelchair, with her black shawl and her rosary, and on the second of June she was sitting at the head of the table, in the middle of the square, next to Graziella, under a white parasol. The two great-grandmothers were more than a hundred and seventy years old between them, as Guido pointed out, since he could do sums faster than anyone. They were holding hands. In front of them, Viola served the first bowl of ribollita of the day, the one she had made herself the Sunday before, with her grandmother’s help and the nepitella leaf added with her own hands. She served it to Assunta, as Graziella had promised in Naples. Assunta tasted it slowly, watched by three hundred people who had stopped talking. Then she looked up at Viola and said something that made the whole square laugh. “Better than your grandmother’s,” she said. “But don’t tell her.” Graziella, beside her, raised her hands. “I told you so,” she answered. “She’s better than me.”

The speeches were few and short, because Graziella had set a rule: whoever spoke for more than two minutes had to wash the dishes. The mayor spoke for one minute fifty seconds, watching the clock. Valeria Conti said the trattoria was proof that a neighbourhood isn’t made of houses, but of people. Mancini read out the headline he would put in the Gazzetta the next day: “Eighty years old, and doesn’t feel it”. Bellini raised his glass and said a single sentence: “You work for those who need it, not for those who can pay more”, and added that his grandfather had written it in 1946, but that in via Maggio they had put it into practice better than he had. Karl said in Florentine, with a terrible Maltese accent and a perfect gorgia, “Grazie, bimbi”, and the square applauded for a full minute. Matei spoke in Romanian to Ion and Doina, and Giulia translated. Ion replied in his 1990 Italian and said that the train had arrived on time that day, for the first time in forty years. Then Graziella stood up. The square fell silent. Graziella looked at the table, sixty metres long, full of faces. She opened her mouth. And said only: “Eat, it’s getting cold.”

Before dessert arrived, Andrei stood up from the table and asked for silence. He said, in an Italian that was by now almost perfect, with every preposition in its place, that Ioana wanted to give the trattoria a present. Ioana took her violin out of its case, stood on a chair in the middle of the square, and played. She played “Florile dalbe”, the carol Ion sang every Christmas, and then, without stopping, a slow melody nobody recognised except Matei and Doina. It was the lullaby of Viorica, Doina’s mother, the one Matei sang to Viola at night, the one Doina had hummed in front of the portrait with the blue veil at the Brukenthal. Andrei had had her learn it specially, in secret, recording it on his phone from Doina at Christmas. Doina covered her face with her hands. Matei stood motionless, his eyes closed. And Viola, who had woken up on Assunta’s knees, began to sing softly, in Romanian, the words her dad had taught her, in the thin voice of a seven-year-old. In piazza Santo Spirito, for three minutes, three hundred people who didn’t understand Romanian stayed silent and listened. There was no need to understand. It was one of those things that are understood the same way in every language.

Then she sat down, and the square burst into applause that could be heard all the way to the Ponte Vecchio. It was the shortest and most beautiful speech of the day, and Mancini put it on the front page the next day, under the headline. They ate until evening. They ate Karl’s ribollita and Viola’s, Karl’s mother’s pastizzi, Doina’s sarmale, Rita’s culurgiones, Assunta’s ragù cooked by Rosaria, don Paolo’s cantucci, Ion’s cozonac. They toasted with Chianti wine and Ion’s pălincă, which made half the square cough. At sunset, when the sun began to sink behind the façade of Santo Spirito, Graziella got up from the table, took Doina’s shawl and asked Pietro to come with her for a moment. Not to the terrace. To the trattoria. They went in through the door on via Maggio, into the empty, silent dining room, with the chairs upturned on the tables because everyone was in the square. Graziella went into the kitchen. She stopped in front of the window above the sink, where Aldo’s plant, in the orange light of sunset, looked like copper. She stayed there, watching the sunset from that window, the one from which, for fifty years, she had never watched it.

Pietro asked her what she was thinking about. Graziella didn’t answer at once. Then she said she was thinking about her father and mother, who had opened that kitchen eighty years before without knowing what it would become. That she was thinking about Aldo, who had arrived with wrecked hands and a loaf of bread, and without whom none of this would have existed. That if Aldo hadn’t come in 1966, there wouldn’t have been three hundred people in the square that day. That she was thinking about everyone who had come through that door in eighty years, the poor and the rich, tourists and neighbours, mud angels and restorers, a Romanian with a notebook, a woman from Sorrento with her brushes, a Maltese man soaked to the skin, a little girl with a thimble. And that every one of them had been fed. Then she turned to Pietro. She said she had heard he was writing a book about via Maggio, and that Bellini had told her he didn’t yet know how to end it. Pietro blushed and admitted it was true. Graziella smiled. “Then I’ll tell you how it ends,” she said. “It doesn’t end. Write it like that. That whoever comes in gets fed. And that the door stays open.”

They went back to the square when it was already dark. The festival lights had come on among the plane trees, like fireflies hung on wires, and someone had brought an accordion. Ion and Doina were teaching everyone to dance the hora, in an enormous circle that turned around the fountain, with Andrei and Ioana, Karl and his mother, Davide and Rita, Guido, who danced like a boy, and even Dr Neri, who kept looking at his watch. Bianca came over to Pietro, took his hand and pulled him into the circle. Pietro danced badly, as always, treading on everyone’s toes. Under the white parasol, Graziella and Assunta watched the circle, hand in hand, with Viola asleep on Assunta’s knees, the silver thimble still on her thumb. Bellini sat beside them, his hat on his knees. Matei and Giulia danced in each other’s arms, slowly, out of time, as on the evening of their wedding under the lemon trees of Sorrento. And Marco and Sara watched them, and every now and then looked at Pietro and Bianca, and exchanged a smile. Pietro, turning in the circle, saw all those faces go by, one after another, like the pages of a book leafed through in a hurry. He thought he knew them all. And that each one had a story.

That night, back home, Pietro didn’t sleep. He sat down at his desk, switched on the lamp and opened Bellini’s black notebook at the last empty page. It was the third black notebook by now: the first two were full, on the bookshelf, next to Bellini’s book, the Crusca’s letter, the dictionary of collocations and Bianca’s green book. On the first page of the first notebook was still the date Bellini had given it to him, the fourth of November 2026, and the sentence he had written: “Carry on. Stories don’t end, they change hands.” Pietro reread that sentence. Then he thought of everything that had happened since. Malta and Totò’s T. The mud and the Madonna. The Crusca and Viola. The angel who laughs. Jupiter’s moons. The third day. The words that are disappearing. The apron hung on the nail. The flower come home. He thought that four years earlier, when he had received the first notebook, he wouldn’t have been able to tell any of this, not with those words. That he had learned to tell stories by telling them. The way you learn to make ribollita by making it. The way you learn to look by looking.

Then he picked up his pen and wrote the last page. Not of the notebook, which still had many pages: of the book. He wrote it in one go, without crossing anything out, for the first time in his life. He wrote: “In via Maggio, in Florence, there is a trattoria that is eighty years old. Above the kitchen door a blue eye is painted, like on the boats of Malta. On the windowsill there is a nepitella plant that came from Bologna in a yoghurt pot on a wedding day in 1975. On a nail by the door hangs an apron that nobody takes down. Upstairs there is a door frame full of notches, which is read from the bottom up. And on the front door there is a rule, written nowhere but known to everyone: whoever comes in gets fed. This is the story of that door. It doesn’t end. If one day you pass through via Maggio, go in. Order the ribollita. Let yourself be hugged. And then, when you come out, if you see a child, take them by the hand, bring them in front of something beautiful, and say to them a single word.” Pietro stopped. He looked at the page. Then he wrote the last word, at the bottom, on its own, in the middle of the line: “Guarda.”
Che cosa ha cambiato Karl nella cucina?
Pochissimo: un piatto maltese il venerdì e un occhio azzurro sulla porta
Chi rimette il fiore nella cornice a Napoli?
Viola lo porta, la restauratrice lo incolla
Che cosa dice Viola davanti all’angelo?
«Ride perché sa che lo stiamo guardando»
Qual è il discorso di Graziella alla festa?
Although she was tired, she wanted to see everything.
The last page of Pietro’s book. Read and answer.
In via Maggio, in Florence, there is a trattoria that is eighty years old.
On the windowsill there is a nepitella plant that came from Bologna in a yoghurt pot, in 1975.
On the door there is a rule written nowhere: whoever comes in gets fed.
If you see a child, bring them in front of something beautiful, and say to them a single word: look.
Da dove è arrivata la nepitella?
Qual è l’ultima parola del libro?
My journey from A1 to B2

I used a mixed conditional (Se non avessi cominciato…, oggi non…).
I used the sequence of tenses (Pensavo che sarebbe stato…, Temevo che fosse…).
I used at least three implicit forms (pur essendo, dopo aver…, finito il…).
I used argumentative connectors and an indefinite concession (qualunque cosa…).
I used at least one word I invented myself, well formed.
When I started, I couldn’t even say “buongiorno”. I thought I’d never reach B2.
If I hadn’t studied every day, today I couldn’t read a story in Italian.
Although I had difficult moments, I never thought of giving up.
Whatever happens, from now on I’ll carry on: the next goal is C1.
